summary: Defines TLS 1.3 cipher suites that provide authentication and integrity using HMAC but do not encrypt the data. They are not for general use, but can suit Internet of Things and constrained settings where confidentiality is not needed and cost matters. The document includes examples of such use cases. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a message does not need to be secret, just proven unchanged. This sends a postcard with a seal that shows nobody altered it.

questions: when do you not need tls encryption
subtitle: TLS 1.3 cipher suites for authentication without encryption

tldr.problem: Many Internet of Things (IoT) and industrial devices need to verify that messages are authentic and unchanged, but do not need to keep the data secret. Standard TLS provides both confidentiality and authentication, which adds overhead and complexity.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9150 defines two TLS 1.3 cipher suites that use HMAC (Hashed Message Authentication Code) to authenticate and protect the integrity of messages without encrypting them. The cipher suites are named TLS_SHA256_SHA256 and TLS_SHA384_SHA384.
tldr.outcome: Devices in closed systems or specific industrial settings can use TLS-based authentication without the computational cost of encryption, but with the important caveat that the approach lacks IETF endorsement and is only suitable where confidentiality is genuinely not needed.

today: RFC 9150 is an Informational document published in April 2022 and remains current. It is not an IETF standards track document and is not IETF-endorsed. The cipher suites it defines are registered with IANA but marked as not recommended for general use. They remain available for specific use cases in constrained or closed systems where confidentiality is genuinely not needed.

sections.title: When You Want Authentication Without Secrecy
sections.content:
Normally, TLS provides both confidentiality and authentication: it keeps data secret and proves that messages have not been tampered with. But some applications do not need secrecy.

Consider a robot arm on a factory floor receiving commands to move a certain distance at a certain speed. An attacker could modify those commands to cause physical damage. But the commands themselves are not secret; anyone could see that the arm was told to move. Similarly, time synchronization data sent to time-sensitive equipment is public information, but must not be modified. Weather information is not confidential, but must be authentic.

In these cases, the overhead of encrypting the data is wasted effort. IoT devices with limited processing power benefit from skipping encryption. This document defines TLS 1.3 cipher suites that provide authentication and integrity checking via HMAC without encrypting the data.

The document is informational and carries an important caveat: this approach is not endorsed by the IETF. It should only be used in closed systems or very specific scenarios where confidentiality is genuinely not needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Some machines need to know a message is real but do not care if someone else reads it. These cipher suites prove a message is real without hiding it.

sections.title: Industrial and IoT Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC describes five concrete use cases where authentication without encryption makes sense.

Robotic manufacturing: A robot arm in a car factory receives commands from a control system. The movements are not trade secrets; the commands are just technical instructions for repetitive tasks. But an attacker modifying the commands could damage equipment. Authentication is critical; encryption is not.

Time synchronization: Motion control systems rely on precise time updates to coordinate. Time information is public, and disclosing it poses no security risk. But modifying time data could cause equipment to fail or move incorrectly. Latency must be very low, so anything that reduces overhead helps.

Alarm reporting: Industrial sensors report alarms when conditions go out of tolerance (for example, temperature too high). The alarm data is not sensitive—anyone could observe the physical condition. But an attacker could trigger false alarms or cover up real ones. Many sensors are power-constrained devices that might not afford the cost of encryption.

Railway interlocking: Commands to railway equipment do not need confidentiality; the position of track switches is publicly known. But integrity is vital: an attacker modifying a command could cause a train to derail. Flight data recording of this traffic must be readable by third parties analyzing safety, which means encryption would prevent the analysis.

Aircraft and ground communication: Pilots exchange route updates, weather information, and other data with ground control. Much of this is not confidential; state and position information is generally known. But modifying this data could cause aircraft to follow wrong routes or give false information to control towers. Authenticity protects against tampering threats.
sections.plainLanguage: Factories, power plants, trains, and airplanes all have systems where commands must be real but do not need to be secret. These use cases show why.

sections.title: How Authentication-Only Cipher Suites Work
sections.content:
The two cipher suites defined in the RFC are TLS_SHA256_SHA256 and TLS_SHA384_SHA384. The names show that they use the same hash function for both the record protection mechanism and the key derivation.

Normal TLS uses AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) algorithms that encrypt and authenticate a message in one operation. These cipher suites replace that with plain HMAC. The record payload is not encrypted; instead, an HMAC authentication tag is appended to the plaintext message. The HMAC is computed over the message, a nonce, and some additional data.

Key lengths and initialization vectors follow the hash output size: TLS_SHA256_SHA256 uses 32-byte keys and IVs, while TLS_SHA384_SHA384 uses 48 bytes.

The handshake and certificate exchange still use the same TLS 1.3 mechanisms for authentication and key agreement. Only the record layer—the part that sends and receives encrypted data—differs. The record data is not encrypted; it is accompanied by an HMAC that receivers can use to detect tampering.

Because the data is not encrypted, the handshake messages and certificates are also sent in plaintext (though with HMAC protection). This is a significant security implication: anyone observing the TLS handshake can read the server certificate and any client certificate or authentication information.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of scrambling the message, the cipher suites add a seal (a hash) to prove the message was not changed. The seal is computed from the message, the key, and some random data.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Implications
sections.content:
The lack of encryption introduces several important constraints:

No confidentiality: All data sent via TLS is visible in plaintext, including handshake messages, certificates, and application data. Any sensitive information, such as bearer tokens in HTTP, must never be sent using these cipher suites.

Unencrypted handshake: Server and client certificates are sent without encryption, only with HMAC integrity protection. Any observer can see certificate contents.

No Pre-Shared Key confidentiality: If using PSK (Pre-Shared Key) authentication, the PSK must not be sent in the handshake. PSKs can only be loaded externally.

Sequence number exposure (DTLS only): In DTLS 1.3, record sequence numbers are normally encrypted to prevent certain attacks. These cipher suites do not encrypt them, so they are exposed.

Key usage limits: Standard TLS defines key usage limits for AEAD ciphers based on cryptanalysis of those algorithms. HMAC has different security properties. Implementations should rotate keys before reaching key usage limits, following general HMAC security guidelines.

No confidentiality by default: These cipher suites must never be the default choice. Devices must be explicitly configured to allow them. Misconfiguration could lead to data being sent unencrypted when the operator believed it was encrypted.

Application protocol assumptions: Protocols like HTTP may assume TLS provides confidentiality. Using these cipher suites with HTTP would violate that assumption. Applications must be aware of the lack of encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risks are that anyone can read the data and that misconfiguration might send secret information unencrypted. These cipher suites are only safe if you truly do not care who reads the messages.

sections.title: Status and Deployment
sections.content:
RFC 9150 is an Informational document published in April 2022 as an independent submission. It is not an IETF standard and does not have IETF consensus or endorsement. The RFC itself states: "The approach described in this document is not endorsed by the IETF and does not have IETF consensus."

The two cipher suites defined (TLS_SHA256_SHA256 and TLS_SHA384_SHA384) have been registered with IANA as valid TLS cipher suites, but are marked as "not recommended." They are available for use in constrained or closed systems where the use case genuinely does not require confidentiality.

Because this is an independent submission without IETF backing, implementors should be cautious about deploying these cipher suites without thorough threat modeling and analysis. The document explicitly requires users to perform a threat analysis before deploying integrity-only cipher suites.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an informational document that describes how to do something, not a recommendation to do it. It is available for very specific use cases but should not be the default approach.
